newsitem.title: UK: Excerpts from UK Clarke's statement on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Excerpts from UK Clarke's statement on EMU.

text.p: Following are excerpts from a parliamentary statement on European economic and monetary union by UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke:

"Over the last few days a number of highly misleading claims have been made about the draft legislation for the detailed preparation of EMU. These culminated in the misrepresentation of a series of documents in yesterday's Sunday Times.

"I am strongly in favour of full parliamentary debate and scrutiny of these important issues. That scrutiny must be properly completed before any decisions are taken which might have binding effect on this country."
Leader of the Commons Tony Newton would make an announcement on the "form and timing" of the debate ahead of the Dublin Euro-summit next month.
"I repeat that no binding decisions will be taken in any forum until that debate has taken place."

"In the light of all the fears that have been expressed, I can assure you that I will seek to come back with the best possible text that puts absolutely beyond doubt what I already believe to be the case...I agree it has to be seen to be copper-botttomed, or as copper-bottomed as we can get it."

"Unless we join stage three of EMU, we will retain, as now, control of domestic economic policy...There is no question of any fines or other sanctions being imposed upon us for running an excessive deficit."
"The opt out from EMU that the Prime Minister negotiated at Maastricht remains entirely unaffected."
"Sterling is now a floating currency. I have no intention of shadowing any currency as long as it remains floating. It would be damaging and futile to do so."

The Government believed "complying with those convergence programmes -- if we do, and that's a matter for us -- is a sign of economic health, whether or not anybody ever thought of a single currency in the first place".
"Everything contained in the EU stability pact -- including fines on "ins' -- derives and was foreshadowed in the Maastricht Treaty."
The Stability Pact made "good economic sense" for the UK and Europe as a means of making sure that EMU was soundly based "whether we are in or out of a single currency.

"If we are in, we need to ensure that no other member of EMU falls into excessive deficit or debt crisis, which might tend to drive up interest rates. If we are out, we need the Euro-zone to be stable as the British economy is more successful when the economies of our major customers are successful."
"That is why I am negotiating so toughly in Ecofin in British interests to get the details right. That is why Parliament must scrutinise properly what I am doing."
Asked if he would veto the stability pact regulations unless Britain had an explicit guarantee that it would be excluded from them, Clarke replied:
"I will certainly veto or vote in every way to confirm the policies I have already described."

He hoped that he had come away with good deals for Britain from previous meetings: "But I won't come away with the best deal if this House insists on proposing total constraints on any movement whatever from any position I take up.

"Since the scrutiny procedure will not have been completed by the time of the Ecofin Council of Ministers meets on Monday, I shall maintain a scrutiny reserve at that meeting. There is nothing new or exceptional about that...That means that nothing of substance can be settled at next Monday's Ecofin meeting."
It was highly unlikely that a stability pact would be decided at next Monday's meeting.
"It will not be concluded next Monday, it was highly unlikely ever to be concluded next Monday. I'm not even sure it will be concluded at Dublin."
"The Maastricht opt-out remains completely untouched by what we are considering. It will remain completely untouched."

On Monday's Ecofin meeting, he said: "I do not expect and I never have expected any items of EMU legislation to come up for formal adoption. We will, however, seek in good faith to reach a broad measure of political agreement."
-- Richard Murphy, London Newsroom 44 171 542 2774
